power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Characterising individual differences in behaviour and predicting future behaviour are central goals of psychological science.
However, behavioural data are difficult to obtain, and most research relies on nomothetic approaches that aggregate them into summary statistics.
This aggregation obscures person-specific patterns that would afford an idiographic understanding of individual behaviour.

Pervasive digital technologies (e.g., smartphones, wearables, and computer-mediated systems) now generate fine-grained, temporally ordered records of everyday behaviour, creating unprecedented opportunities to study both systematic inter-individual differences and patterns of intra-individual variation in digital behaviour.
Here, we introduce Natural Behaviour Processing (NBP) as a framework for analysing digital behavioural data using sequence modelling approaches adapted from natural language processing.

We argue that behaviour shares structural properties with language: both involve a repository of possible actions (vocabulary), systematic patterns governing how elements typically combine (grammar), and context-dependent meaning (semantics).
These structural parallels motivate applying sequencebased models, which have revolutionised language processing, to the study of behaviour more broadly.

We provide a brief illustrative review of pioneering studies demonstrating that sequential approaches capture person-specific patterns that aggregation loses, across topics including life outcomes, decision making, social media use, consumer behaviour, digital education, and health.

We discuss the challenges facing NBP adoption, including the tension between predictive modelling and theoretical understanding, the need for large-scale curated behaviour datasets, and methodological training requirements.

By modelling the order and context of everyday actions rather than aggregates, NBP could enable person-specific representations of behaviour that support both individual-level prediction and systematic comparison of individual differences across people.

text.text: Pervasive digital technologies (e.g., smartphones, wearables) and computer-mediated systems (e.g., social networks, AI agents) now mediate much of everyday human activity, drastically changing behaviour and our ability to study it.

The detailed records of behaviour generated by these digital technologies provide unprecedented opportunities for psychologists to investigate behaviour in-situ, longitudinally, and at a previously unseen scale and granularity [8] [9] [10].

text.text: Yet analysing such data still poses several challenges.
Here, we address one of them: combining nomothetic and idiographic modelling of digital behaviour.

Most studies in psychology focus on nomothetic analytic approaches (i.e., techniques that average across people or within persons to obtain average effects meant to generalise at the population level), rather than idiographic approaches (i.e., techniques that model individual dynamics within a person to describe person-level effects meant to generalise only at the individual level) [11, 12].

text.text: What is needed are frameworks that capture both fine-grained, person-specific patterns in everyday digital behaviour and the individual differences that characterise people within a population.

Inspired by sequence modelling approaches, often used for the analysis of verbal behaviour via language data, here we introduce the term Natural Behaviour Processing (NBP) as a parallel framework for approaching sequence modelling of digital behaviour via other sources of data (e.g., mobile sensing, screenshots, digital footprints).
Sequence modelling has long been used in speech and signal processing [e.g., 22].

Transformer models, a class of sequence models that learn how each element of a sequence relates to every other element, allowing them to capture context-dependent meaning, have dramatically improved natural language processing (NLP) in recent years [see 23, for an introduction], and their potential for psychology is widely recognised [24].

text.text: The NBP approach similarly aims to account for the sequentially structured, dynamic, and context-dependent nature of individual behaviours by avoiding aggregation and relying on the natural structure inherent in discrete digital behavioural data.
In what follows, we employ the useful yet imperfect "language of behaviour " analogy to outline structural similarities between NBP and NLP.

We then review illustrative studies that have applied sequential approaches to behavioural data, highlighting their idiographic and nomothetic insights, and conclude with challenges and future directions for NBP research.
For many readers, it will not come as a surprise that language, often considered a form of verbal behaviour [19], shares similarities in structure with other forms of behaviour (Figure 1).

text.text: Many forms of behaviour are temporal in nature, have hierarchical sequential structural elements, and show connections and dependencies [25, 26].

text.text: Given these similarities, psychologists should characterise not just what people do but how they do it (e.g., in which order, in how many steps, and in how many variations an action is completed).

For example, information is ingrained in how acts are interconnected in an immediate sense (e.g., using one's phone to check social media consists of an unlock-tap-scroll sequence) and may relate to other processes across temporal and situational contexts (e.g., the formation of social media habits).
Behaviour is not equivalent to language.
But language use is a form of verbal behaviour that bridges covert cognition with overt actions (e.g., expressions).
Behaviour, considered more generally, can be communicative (e.g., non-verbal gestures), but unlike language, communication need not be a primary function.
Still, many behaviours share critical structural properties with the expression of verbal behaviour in language: they share temporal ordering, hierarchical organisation, and context-dependence.
It is these structural parallels, rather than functional equivalence, that motivate the NBP analogy, which we believe can be a useful approach for studying individual (digital) behaviour.
First, language has a "vocabulary": the words and phrases that are common in a language, its dialects and variants, and the usage of individuals and groups.
When it comes to other forms of behaviour, we argue that a repository of behavioural actions serves as an equivalent to vocabulary that comprises the possible actions that an individual might enact.

The size of this act repository can depend on past experience and learning, momentary physical and psychological states (e.g., fatigue or anxiety), stable dispositions and abilities, and the affordances of the situation.

Much like people with larger vocabularies can communicate with a greater number and variation of words, individuals with larger act repositories should be able to exhibit more complex behaviours in different situations (e.g., beginner vs. experienced social media users).
One core difference between verbal behaviour as encoded in language and many other behaviours is that, in language, the unit of analysis seems naturally given.
Intuitively, language seems to come already divided into words.

What counts as a "word" differs across languages and cannot be defined consistently [27]; in Turkish or Finnish, for example, a single word can express what English expresses in a whole phrase (e.g., Finnish taloissammekin, "in our houses, too").

text.text: Accordingly, current NLP models do not operate on whole words.
Instead, they learn a vocabulary of frequently recurring text fragments directly from data (so-called subword tokens, e.g., "walk" and "-ing" in "walking") [23].
text.formatted: Instead, they learn a vocabulary of frequently recurring text fragments directly from data (so-called subword tokens, e.g., "walk" and "-ing" in "walking") <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[23]</ref>.

text.text: As NBP approaches are adopted to model different digital behaviours, researchers will need to determine whether a behavioural "act" should be, for example, a tap of the screen, an app launch, a usage session (e.g., all use from screen activation to deactivation), or a labelled media use activity (e.g., watching a video).

Act repositories can therefore be specified in top-down and bottom-up ways, including from a theoretical standpoint, derived empirically by learning characteristic recurring units from data, or pragmatically imposed by the measurement instrument (e.g., mobile sensing software being used).

In NBP, researchers will need to justify these choices in light of their research question, data, and measurement, and test how sensitive their findings are to them, including which acts enter the act repository.
Second, we can consider the "grammar" of behaviour through systematic patterns of behavioural acts that constrain and structure typical behaviour for functionality.

Just as linguistic grammar determines how words can be meaningfully arranged into sentences, behavioural patterns could be construed as equivalent to grammar in that they represent how actions are ordered to be functional.
While not as strictly defined as within language, behaviour is structured.
For example, when it comes to digital behaviour, we log into our email account before we start to write a message; we unlock a phone before opening an app and taking a photo.

Much like words in sentences and sentences in texts, these behavioural sequences hierarchically nest within larger units: individual acts (e.g., unlocking a phone) combine into behavioural episodes (e.g., a messaging session), episodes into habits that recur across days (e.g., checking messages upon waking), and habits into routines and lifestyles that characterise patterns over weeks, months, or even years.
Third, a parallel can be drawn with respect to "semantics" in language when we consider the cultural, social, or psychological meaning of behavioural acts within situations.
For example, smiling behaviour may indicate happiness in one situation but nervousness or sarcasm in another [21].
text.formatted: For example, smiling behaviour may indicate happiness in one situation but nervousness or sarcasm in another <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[21]</ref>.

text.text: Checking your phone may reflect boredom, anxiety, or genuine urgency, depending on the surrounding circumstances.

Thus, behavioural acts are specifically meaningful within the psychological situation experienced by the person [20, 28, 29], just as words derive meaning from their sentential, conversational, cultural, or social context.
text.formatted: Thus, behavioural acts are specifically meaningful within the psychological situation experienced by the person <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">28,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">29]</ref>, just as words derive meaning from their sentential, conversational, cultural, or social context.

text.text: Given that behaviour shares significant structural properties with language, methodological ap- proaches that have catalysed the study of language may largely generalise to behaviour more broadly.

For example, large language models (i.e., transformers; [30]) excel at language processing tasks because they can capture bidirectional dependencies and contextual meaning in sequential dataproperties that characterise language use as much as many other behaviours.
text.formatted: For example, large language models (i.e., transformers; <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[30]</ref>) excel at language processing tasks because they can capture bidirectional dependencies and contextual meaning in sequential dataproperties that characterise language use as much as many other behaviours.

text.text: Large behaviour models (LBMs), built like large language models (LLMs), might enable a similar progression.

Returning to the discussion on nomothetic and idiographic research approaches, an LBM trained across many individuals could be considered nomothetic, even when it carries person-level embeddings: it learns general regularities of intra-individual dynamics.

Its idiographic value lies in what those learnt representations afford for the single case (e.g., prediction of actions, characterisation of influential events, illustration of behavioural sequences).
We now turn to an illustrative review of empirical work that highlights its potential.

Sequence modelling of behavioural data has not yet been widely adopted in psychology, but pioneering work in adjacent fields, especially in applied settings, can inspire research and adoption in the field of psychology.
In application, sequence models are optimised for task accuracy, and the personlevel structure they learn is a by-product.
The NBP approach treats that structure as the object of study and asks what it reveals about individuals.

text.text: Past work used sequence models to computationally represent dynamic patterns in human behaviour for the prediction of plausible future actions [e.g., social media use 31], decisions [e.g., customer churn 32], and important life outcomes [e.g., diseases 33] for individuals and populations.

The NBP framework we propose here extends this logic to the intermediate timescale of everyday naturalistic behaviour: the continuous stream of different actions, communications, and movements that constitute daily life, observed across different behavioural domains (e.g., communication, mobility) and situations.

One challenge of NBP is the alignment of a more predictive sequential framework with the need for a better theoretical understanding of the psychological functions and processes that underlie behaviour [21].
text.formatted: One challenge of NBP is the alignment of a more predictive sequential framework with the need for a better theoretical understanding of the psychological functions and processes that underlie behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[21]</ref>.

text.text: The adoption of transformer models has revolutionised the way language data can be processed but has not generated an equally large leap forward in understanding the cognitive underpinnings of language [44, 45], nor a level of transparency in outputs that would enable us to do so.
text.formatted: The adoption of transformer models has revolutionised the way language data can be processed but has not generated an equally large leap forward in understanding the cognitive underpinnings of language <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">[44,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">45]</ref>, nor a level of transparency in outputs that would enable us to do so.

text.text: NBP is therefore likely to be directly useful for descriptive and predictive work wherever sequential structure holds information beyond aggregates, while its utility for explanatory work remains an open empirical question.

Within NBP, theory can enter at several points: in deriving research questions, specifying act repositories, and interpreting what a model has learnt, so that results are insightful rather than a black-box output.
Mechanistic interpretability (methods that examine how a model arrives at its outputs) could help extend NBP towards causal investigations.
As a model processes a sequence, it forms internal representations: patterns of activity that summarise what the preceding acts signal, loosely comparable to latent variables in psychological models.
Causal tracing, for instance, applies the logic of mediation analysis to these representations, testing which of them carry the effect of an input on a prediction [46].
text.formatted: Causal tracing, for instance, applies the logic of mediation analysis to these representations, testing which of them carry the effect of an input on a prediction <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">[46]</ref>.

text.text: Suppose an LBM predicts that a person will open a social media app, and causal tracing shows that this prediction depends on a representation the model forms during idle waiting periods.
Replacing it with the representation from a busy period should suppress the prediction.

If it does, the finding yields a testable hypothesis: a brief prompt shown during idle periods, before a social media app launches, should reduce app use, as field experiments with self-nudging apps suggest [47].
text.formatted: If it does, the finding yields a testable hypothesis: a brief prompt shown during idle periods, before a social media app launches, should reduce app use, as field experiments with self-nudging apps suggest <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">[47]</ref>.

text.text: In principle, the sequential format of NBP aligns with the goal of studying individual differences in psychological processes over time (i.e., by providing a dynamic temporal order of events).
Pretrained models are also likely to partly encode or approximate underlying psychological processes implicitly.
This can be tested by removing parts of the input or model (ablation) and by evaluating models in new domains or populations (generalisation) [36, 48].
text.formatted: This can be tested by removing parts of the input or model (ablation) and by evaluating models in new domains or populations (generalisation) <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[36,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">48]</ref>.

text.text: Related techniques, such as event masking and anomaly detection, can hint at data-generating processes and inform confirmatory research [35].
text.formatted: Related techniques, such as event masking and anomaly detection, can hint at data-generating processes and inform confirmatory research <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[35]</ref>.

text.text: Hence, if used for more than improving predictive performance, which would be valuable in itself [49], NBP could represent a useful intermediary step [16, 19] towards a psychological science that can characterise individuals relative to their population.
text.formatted: Hence, if used for more than improving predictive performance, which would be valuable in itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">[49]</ref>, NBP could represent a useful intermediary step <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">19]</ref> towards a psychological science that can characterise individuals relative to their population.

text.text: Research on LLMs has also revealed that their performance largely depends on jointly scaling model and training-data size [50].
text.formatted: Research on LLMs has also revealed that their performance largely depends on jointly scaling model and training-data size <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[50]</ref>.

text.text: Whether such scaling relationships transfer to digital behaviour is an open empirical question: behavioural logs are far more platform-dependent and heterogeneous than text, so comparable data may be much scarcer than raw volume suggests.
If they do transfer, the data volume will become a critical bottleneck.

Outside of industry, psychology mostly lacks the data infrastructure to meet this challenge, and the field is fragmented into myriad constructs and measures [51], often studied through isolated small-scale investigations focused on in-sample effects that lack generalisability [52].
text.formatted: Outside of industry, psychology mostly lacks the data infrastructure to meet this challenge, and the field is fragmented into myriad constructs and measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[51]</ref>, often studied through isolated small-scale investigations focused on in-sample effects that lack generalisability <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[52]</ref>.

text.text: A path forward could be to consolidate efforts around large, curated datasets of specific contextualised behaviours [e.g., cognitive experiments, life trajectories 35, 36], enabling LBMs that generalise across behavioural domains (see Table 1).

text.text: This will require large-scale collaborations across labs and building methodological capacity among graduate and postgraduate researchers.
Scientific theories evolve alongside the methods and tools of a discipline [53].
text.formatted: Scientific theories evolve alongside the methods and tools of a discipline <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">[53]</ref>.

text.text: In psychology, for example, Galton's application of regression and Spearman's factor analysis preceded hierarchical models such as the Big Five personality taxonomy [54].
text.formatted: In psychology, for example, Galton's application of regression and Spearman's factor analysis preceded hierarchical models such as the Big Five personality taxonomy <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">[54]</ref>.

text.text: In the same way, NBP and increasingly granular data could transform how we operationalise and conceptualise human behaviour.

We expect NBP to be adopted widely in the next few years, bringing a period of methodological learning: mapping digital artefacts to behaviour, integrating theory, standardising analytic approaches, and mindfully engaging with open science principles when working with privacy-sensitive data.
